edbDesc: An attractive property of the surface of a liquid. It is what causes the surface portion of liquid to be attracted to another surface, such as that of another portion of liquid (as in connecting bits of water or as in a drop of mercury that forms a cohesive ball).
title: Surface tension
description: A liquid's surface behaves like a stretched skin, pulling drops round and holding up light objects. Young explained it, and how it sets whether a liquid wets a surface, in 1805; it shapes the droplets fired by inkjet printers, and soaps work by weakening it so water can soak into cloth.
effect: the surface of a liquid pulls tight like a stretched skin
usedIn: Shot towers dropping molten lead into round shot
strength: Water's skin holds up a dry steel needle or a pond skater, a pull of about 0.07 newtons along each metre of edge.
pickWhy: Specific effect the deck lacks; Segner named the idea in 1751 but Young's 1805 essay is the standard explanation. Wetting merges here.
